question: A pro-vaping post shared this chart of American high-school pupils: vapes rising as cigarettes fall, a perfect swap. Where's the trick?
answer: In the two scales, which make a 26-point rise look the size of a 10-point fall. On one axis, far more teenagers took up vapes than gave up cigarettes. And smoking was falling before vapes: from 28% of high-school pupils in 2000 to 16% in 2011. A swap needs the same people on both lines.
move: Before calling one thing a replacement, check the sizes match on one scale.
ask: When something new seems to replace something old, do I check it is not simply adding to it?

scene.headline: Vapes are replacing cigarettes
scene.label: US high-school pupils using, %
scene.found: Yes: each line has its own scale, so the swings look equal.
scene.miss: That part is fair. Compare the numbers on the two sides.

misses.headline: That's the claim to test. The drawing is what sells it.
misses.marks: Each line is drawn right for its own axis. Do they share one?

scene.name: Two scales, one swap
scene.lesson: Two scales can make any rise mirror any fall. On one axis, see which is bigger.

reference: CDC, Tobacco Product Use Among Middle and High School Students, United States, 2011–2019, MMWR reports on the National Youth Tobacco Survey; Wang et al., MMWR 68(50), 2019
